content: Tobramycin is a medication that can cause serious side effects, including hearing loss and kidney damage. Before starting treatment with tobramycin, it is essential to inform your doctor and pharmacist about all the prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially diuretics (commonly referred to as water pills), cisplatin (Platinol), amphotericin (Amphotec, Fungizone), other antibiotics, and any vitamins or supplements. If you experience symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, ringing in the ears, hearing loss, numbness, muscle twitching or weakness, difficulty breathing, decreased urination, rash, itching, or a sore throat, you should contact your healthcare provider immediately. Your doctor has prescribed tobramycin to treat your infection. This antibiotic may be administered either as an injection into a large muscle (such as the buttock or hip) or through an intravenous (IV) infusion, which will drip into your vein over at least 30 minutes, one to three times daily. Tobramycin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including those affecting the lungs, skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and urinary tract. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other uses, so you should consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how well your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting tobramycin, you must inform your doctor if you are allergic to any aminoglycoside antibiotics, such as amikacin, gentamicin (Garamycin), kanamycin (Kantrex), neomycin, netilmicin (Netromycin), streptomycin, or tobramycin itself. Additionally, disclose all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, particularly diuretics, cisplatin, amphotericin, other antibiotics, and vitamins. Inform your doctor if you have a history of kidney disease, vertigo, hearing loss, ringing in the ears, myasthenia gravis, or Parkinson's disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor immediately, as tobramycin can harm the fetus. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor right away. Before administering tobramycin, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it. Do not use the solution if it appears discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is critical to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your treatment prematurely, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. Tobramycin may cause side effects. To minimize the risk, your healthcare provider may adjust your dosage based on blood test results. If you experience symptoms such as an upset stomach, vomiting, fatigue, or pale skin, inform your healthcare provider if these symptoms are severe or persistent. If you develop a severe rash or have difficulty breathing, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects should be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program, either online or by phone. If you are receiving tobramycin intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely provide you with a supply of the medication to store at home. You will probably be instructed to keep it in the refrigerator or freezer. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are storing additional doses in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving tobramycin intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide specific storage instructions. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving tobramycin through an IV or under the skin, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection. Symptoms near the catheter site may include tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. If you notice any of these symptoms, inform your healthcare provider as soon as possible. Tobramycin is also marketed under the brand name Nebcin®.
